text: Once more he took up teaching by the lake, and such a crowd pressed in that he climbed into a boat and sat there just offshore, with everyone else lined up along the beach.
He taught them at length that day using stories, and this is how one of them went:
"Pay attention — a farmer went out to plant.
Scattering the seed as he walked, some of it landed right on the footpath, and birds swooped down and ate it before it could take.
Some landed on a thin skin of soil over rock, and came up fast because the ground underneath gave it nowhere to root.
Then the sun beat down, and having no real root it scorched and died.
Some fell where thorn bushes were already established, and the thorns simply overran it, and it never produced anything.
But some landed on good, deep ground, and it came up and kept growing and produced thirty, sixty, even a hundred times what was planted."
Then he added, "Whoever has ears ought to use them."
Later, once he was away from the crowd, the twelve and the others close to him asked what the stories meant.
He told them, "You've been let in on the secret of God's kingdom, but for people outside this circle it stays in story form —
so that, as it's written, they can look and look without really seeing, and listen and listen without understanding, or they might actually turn and be forgiven."
He went on, "You're missing this one? Then how will you follow any of the others?
The farmer is sowing the message itself.
The footpath cases are people who hear it, and before it can settle, the accuser snatches away whatever was planted in them.
The thin-soil cases hear the word and grab onto it eagerly right away —
but nothing ever roots, so it doesn't last; the moment trouble or opposition shows up over it, they're gone.
Then there are the thorny-ground cases — they hear it too,
but worry over daily life, the lure of wealth, and wanting other things crowd in and strangle the word, so nothing comes of it.
And the good-soil cases are the ones who actually hear it, take it in, and produce — thirty, sixty, a hundred times over."
He asked them, "Does anyone light a lamp just to hide it under a bowl or shove it under the bed? No — you set it up on a stand.
Nothing stays concealed forever; everything hidden eventually comes out into plain view.
If you've got ears, use them."
"Think carefully about what you're hearing," he told them. "Whatever measure you use on others will be used on you — and more besides.
Whoever already has something will be given more; whoever has nothing will lose even that."
He also said, "God's kingdom works like this: someone scatters seed across a field.
Then he goes about his life, sleeping and waking, while the seed sprouts and grows on its own — he couldn't explain how if you asked him.
The ground just produces, on its own timetable: first a shoot, then a head, then the full grain filling it out.
And the moment it's ripe, he's out there with the sickle, because harvest won't wait."
"How else can I describe God's kingdom," he asked, "what story captures it?
Picture a mustard seed — about the tiniest seed you could plant —
yet once it's in the ground it shoots up past every other garden plant, with branches wide enough that birds build nests in its shade."
He kept teaching this way, story after story, pitched to what the crowd could actually take in.
But alone with his own disciples, he spelled every one of them out plainly.
That evening, once the teaching was done, he told them, "Let's cross over to the far side."
So they left the crowd behind and set out with him in the boat, other boats trailing along.
Partway across, a fierce squall blew up, throwing waves over the side until the boat was taking on serious water.
Jesus, meanwhile, was in the back, asleep on a cushion. They shook him awake: "Teacher! Don't you care that we're about to go under?"
He got up, silenced the wind, and told the sea, "Enough — be still." And just like that, the wind dropped and the water went flat calm.
"Why were you so afraid?" he asked them. "Still no faith in you?"
They were more shaken now than during the storm, saying to each other, "Who is this, that even wind and water do what he says?"
